planting.note: Plant grafted or budded trees in spring after frost in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil; Clifford is hardy and productive in zones 9-11 and is self-fruitful, so it does not require a separate male tree.

directions: Clifford originated as a seedling street tree in Riverside, California, and is valued because it is hermaphroditic and self-fruitful, setting heavy, regular crops without needing a separate male pollinator the way most carob trees do. Its pods are light brown, slightly curved, and notably sweet, with a sugar content often cited near 50 percent, ripening in early autumn. Like all carobs it is extremely drought-tolerant once established and performs best in dry, rocky, alkaline soils typical of Mediterranean climates; irrigation during establishment and pod fill improves yield substantially. Harvest pods once they have turned fully brown and dried on the tree, when the seeds rattle audibly inside.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil; Sfax is a female cultivar and needs a male or hermaphroditic carob tree nearby for reliable pod set.

directions: Sfax is a leading Tunisian female carob cultivar prized for its long, fat, dark-brown pods, often 7 to 8 inches long, with very high sugar content that makes them especially sweet and tender for fresh eating and syrup production. Because it is female, Sfax needs a male or hermaphroditic carob such as Clifford planted nearby, since the species is wind-pollinated and largely dioecious. Trees are slow to establish but become extremely long-lived and drought-tolerant, thriving in rocky, alkaline Mediterranean-climate soils where irrigation is minimal. Harvest pods in autumn once they dry to a uniform dark brown and the seeds rattle inside.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Daddow is frost-tender and best suited to zones 10-11, and is valued as a reliable pollenizer for other macadamia cultivars.

directions: Daddow is a long-established Australian macadamia cultivar grown both for its own nut crop and, importantly, as a cross-pollen source that boosts nut set in neighboring macadamia trees of other cultivars. It produces medium-sized, good-quality nuts on a vigorous, wind-tolerant tree, and orchardists commonly interplant it alongside other selections specifically to improve overall block yields through cross-pollination. Like other macadamias it demands consistently warm, frost-free conditions and deep, well-drained soil, with a long juvenile period before significant bearing begins. Water regularly during nut development and harvest mature nuts once they drop naturally from the tree.
sources: Queensland Department of Primary Industries macadamia variety reference

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil; Akbari is a late-flowering female cultivar and needs a compatible male pollinator blooming at the same time.

directions: Akbari is one of Iran's premier commercial pistachio cultivars, prized for producing an unusually long, elongated nut often marketed as a jumbo or super-long type and commanding a premium price among in-shell pistachios. It flowers later in the season than many other Iranian cultivars, so pollinizer timing matters when siting a compatible male tree nearby. Like Kerman, it needs a long, hot, dry summer with substantial winter chill to fill and split properly, and is poorly suited to humid climates. Plant in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil, expect a long juvenile period before full bearing, and harvest in early autumn once hulls loosen and shells show their characteristic natural split.
sources: Fatty Acids-Based Quality Index to Differentiate Worldwide Commercial Pistachio Cultivars (PMC)
University of California Cooperative Extension — Pistachio Production Manual

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil; Kaleh Ghouchi is an early-flowering female cultivar and needs a compatible male pollinator blooming at the same time.

directions: Kaleh Ghouchi is a major Iranian pistachio cultivar known for its very large, broad, jumbo-shaped nut, distinct from the narrower, elongated shape of Akbari grown in the same regions. It flowers earlier than many other Iranian cultivars, which growers must account for when choosing a compatible male pollinator. It shares the species' demanding requirements for a hot, dry, low-humidity summer and substantial winter chill to properly fill and split its shell, making it a poor fit outside true arid-summer climates. Grow in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil and expect strong biennial bearing once the tree reaches full maturity after several years, harvesting in early autumn as hulls loosen and shells split.
sources: Fatty Acids-Based Quality Index to Differentiate Worldwide Commercial Pistachio Cultivars (PMC)
Assessment of phenolic profile and antioxidant power of five pistachio cultivars from Iran (PMC)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil; Fandoghi is the most widely planted Iranian female cultivar and needs a compatible male pollinator nearby.

directions: Fandoghi, whose name references its rounder, hazelnut-like shape, is the most widely cultivated pistachio variety in Iran and forms the backbone of the country's pistachio industry alongside Akbari, Ohadi, and Kaleh Ghouchi. Its nuts are smaller and rounder than the elongated Akbari type but the tree is valued for consistent, reliable production across a wide range of growing districts. Like other pistachio cultivars it requires a long, hot, arid summer and significant winter chill to develop and split its shell properly, and performs poorly in humid climates. Plant in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil with a compatible male pollinator nearby, and harvest in early autumn once hulls loosen and nuts show their natural shell split.
sources: Fatty Acids-Based Quality Index to Differentiate Worldwide Commercial Pistachio Cultivars (PMC)
University of California Cooperative Extension — Pistachio Production Manual

common_name: Bungo Ume (Large Tart Japanese Apricot for Umeboshi and Umeshu)
subcategory: East Asian ornamental-edible stone fruit tree

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Bungo is named for the historic Japanese province now part of Oita Prefecture and is believed to carry some apricot (Prunus armeniaca) ancestry, giving it larger fruit than many ume selections.

directions: Bungo produces notably large, tart fruit compared to most Japanese apricot cultivars, a trait attributed to possible apricot ancestry mixed into the mume lineage, and is grown both for its showy pink spring blossoms and as a serious fruiting tree for traditional umeboshi, syrups, and umeshu liqueur. It flowers in late winter to early spring on bare wood before leaf-out, like other Prunus mume selections, with fruit ripening from green through gold over late spring into early summer. Because many ume cultivars including Bungo are only partially self-fruitful, plant a second compatible Prunus mume cultivar nearby to ensure a heavy, reliable crop. Prune to an open form after harvest to maintain airflow and fruiting wood, and pick fruit while still firm and green-gold for pickling or let it ripen further for fresh use.
sources: general horticultural reference on Prunus mume cultivars
